quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer: Yes — faint gray text can be a problem because WCAG 2.2 requires a minimum contrast ratio for readable text: Level AA, Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast (Minimum)) requires normal text to have at least 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text), with exceptions for incidental text, inactive UI components, and logotypes [1][3]. Note also that if no background color is specified, white is assumed when measuring contrast [3][4].

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum)): targets for pointer input must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when spaced so a 24‑pixel diameter circle centered on each undersized target does not intersect another target, or when an equivalent control exists on the same page, the target is inline (size constrained by line‑height), the size is determined by the user agent, or a particular presentation is essential or legally required. [2]

Level AAA — Success Criterion 2.5.5 (Target Size (Enhanced)): targets for pointer input must be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, except when an equivalent control exists on the same page, the target is inline, the size is determined by the user agent, or a particular presentation is essential to the information. [1]

Techniques: using CSS (e.g., min-width/min-height) to ensure target size or spacing are documented techniques but are examples, not the only way to satisfy the criteria (see C42 and C44). [3][4]

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer:
- Level AA — Large-scale (large) text: must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 (Success Criterion 1.4.3). [2]  
- Level AA — Icons (user interface components / graphical objects): visual parts required to identify UI components or to understand graphics must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors (Success Criterion 1.4.11). [4]  
- Level AAA — Large-scale (large) text: must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (Success Criterion 1.4.6). [1]

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer:
1.4.3 (Level AA) requires the visual presentation of text and images of text to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (large-scale text and images of large-scale text: at least 3:1), with exceptions for incidental text, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, pictures containing significant other visual content, and logotypes/brand text [1][4].  
1.4.6 (Level AAA) is the enhanced (stricter) contrast requirement at Level AAA (Contrast (Enhanced)) — it raises contrast expectations beyond Level AA (intent described as “Enhanced”) [2].  
1.4.6 guidance also clarifies that heavily stylized text or characters used as symbols may be treated as non‑text content and be evaluated under Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non‑Text Contrast instead [5][2].

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer:
Level AA — SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: Disabled (inactive) user interface components are exempt from the 3:1 non-text contrast requirement, so the text on a disabled button is not required to meet that contrast ratio. [1][4]  
Unless a control is inactive, any visual information (including text or state indicators) necessary to identify or operate the control must meet at least 3:1 contrast with adjacent colors. [5][1]

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer:
Level AA (SC 1.4.11): Logos are exempt from the non-text contrast requirement when a particular presentation is essential (for example, mandated by brand guidelines) [1][3][4]. However, if a logo is used as a user interface component (e.g., a linked logo or control) authors should provide a variant with sufficient contrast or an equivalent control, because the exemption can be problematic in those cases [1][3][4]. If an author deliberately presents a logo with low contrast for stylistic reasons (not because it is essential or required by brand guidelines), that low-contrast presentation is not exempt and must meet the contrast requirement [2][4]. 

Level AAA (SC 1.4.6): Text in logos/logotypes is similarly exempt at AAA, but the same cautions apply when logos act as UI components and when low contrast is an author choice—authors are encouraged to provide higher-contrast variants or equivalent controls [5].

quality.question: Which success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2?
quality.answer: The following success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA) [2]. 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) (AAA) [2]. 2.4.13 Focus Appearance (AAA) [2]. 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA) [2]. 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA) [2]. 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A) [2]. 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A) [2]. 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA) [2]. 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (AAA) [2].

quality.question: Is 4.1.1 Parsing still required?
quality.answer: Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing (Level A, formerly) has been removed and is no longer required. [4][3] The underlying reason given is that assistive technology no longer needs to directly parse HTML, so the criterion no longer has utility. [3][2] Although some Test Rules were defined for aspects of this criterion, they are not necessary for conformance and the criterion itself is obsolete. [5][1]

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.10 requires content to reflow without horizontal scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels [1][2]. 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels at 400% zoom (test guidance also specifies using a 1280px wide viewport at 400% zoom) [1][3][4].

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer:
Level A — Success Criterion 2.3.1 (Three Flashes or Below Threshold): content must be three flashes or below the flash threshold (i.e., not exceed three flashes) [2][3][5].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 2.3.2 (Three Flashes): do not flash content more than 3 times a second [4][3].

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer: Yes — but only if it meets Success Criterion 1.1.1 Non‑text Content (Level A): provide a text alternative that identifies and describes the CAPTCHA’s purpose and provide alternative forms of the CAPTCHA using output modes for different types of sensory perception (i.e., another modality) [1][2]. Techniques include supplying a text alternative that describes the puzzle and ensuring the page offers another CAPTCHA serving the same purpose in a different modality (G143 and G144) [3][4]. The Understanding document also recommends going beyond the minimum: offer more than two modalities, provide human customer‑service bypass, or avoid CAPTCHAs for authorized users [2].

quality.question: minimun constrast for txt
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.3 (Contrast (Minimum)): normal text must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (large-scale text must be at least 3:1); incidental/decorative text, inactive UI text, text not visible to anyone, and logotypes are exempt from the contrast requirement [2].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 1.4.6 (Contrast (Enhanced)): normal text must have a contrast ratio of at least 7:1 (large-scale text must be at least 4.5:1); the same exceptions (incidental/decorative text, inactive UI text, not visible, and logotypes) apply [1].  
Techniques and test rules (examples) for checking these ratios are described in Techniques G18 and G17 respectively [3][4].

quality.question: Quel est le contraste minimum pour le texte ?
quality.answer:
Pour le niveau AA (Succès Critère 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)) : le texte doit avoir un contraste d'au moins 4,5:1 (texte normal) et au moins 3:1 pour le texte en grande taille. [2][5]

Pour le niveau AAA (Succès Critère 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)) : le texte doit avoir un contraste d'au moins 7:1 (texte normal) et au moins 4,5:1 pour le texte en grande taille. [1]

Certaines exceptions s'appliquent (texte purement décoratif, parties inactives de l'interface, non visibles, éléments d'image comportant d'autres contenus significatifs, logotypes), auquel cas il n'y a pas d'exigence de contraste. [1][2]
